weeks.title: Place value to a million

spell.rule: verb prefixes dis-, mis-, re-, de-, over- (disagree, misbehave, reappear, defrost, overflow)

weeks.read: a longer novel of the child's choice from the library, to read through the half term

days.ma: Write digit cards 0–9 on paper scraps; pick six to make a number such as 482,615. Read it aloud, then say the value of every digit (the 8 is worth 80,000).
days.en: Choose a library novel for this half term and start a reading journal: write the title, your first impressions after ten pages and one question you want answered.

days.ma: Use the same six cards to make the largest and smallest possible numbers, then write both in words, e.g. nine hundred and seventy-five thousand, four hundred and twenty-one.
days.en: Read aloud for 10 minutes, then find and label one noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition and determiner on a single page of your book.

days.ma: Order these smallest to largest: 305,412; 350,142; 35,421; 305,241; 530,124. Then write three comparisons using < and >.
days.en: Handwriting: copy two sentences from your book in joined writing, then again a little faster. Circle your neatest joins and decide which letters (e.g. after g, j, y) you prefer not to join.

days.ma: Partition 704,096 in three different ways, e.g. 700,000 + 4,000 + 96 and 704 thousands + 96 ones. Explain what each zero is doing.
days.en: Add dis-, mis-, re-, de- and over- to appear, behave, build, frost and sleep. Write a sentence for each new verb and explain how the prefix changed the meaning.

days.ma: Quick check: write one million in digits; give the value of the 6 in 368,210; order 99,999, 100,001 and 90,999; make the number closest to 500,000 from your digit cards.
days.en: Quick check: tell a parent what has happened in your book so far in five sentences, label the word classes in 'The tired dog slept quietly under the table', and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Counting in powers of 10 and Roman numerals

spell.rule: suffixes that turn nouns and adjectives into verbs: -ate, -ise, -ify (active → activate, apology → apologise, solid → solidify)

weeks.read: a myth or legend from a library collection

days.ma: Start at 45,260 and count on in 1,000s to 53,260 aloud, then count back in 10,000s from 145,260 to 5,260, writing each number.
days.en: Read a myth or legend. List the hero, the challenge, the magical or supernatural element and the ending, then discuss what lesson the story teaches.

days.ma: Write 10 more, 100 more, 1,000 more, 10,000 more and 100,000 more than 489,905. Circle any place where several digits change at once.
days.en: Find three descriptions of a creature or hero in the myth. Turn a plain phrase into an expanded noun phrase: 'the dragon' → 'the ancient, smoke-breathing dragon with scales like rusted armour'.

days.ma: Learn I, V, X, L, C, D and M. Write 1–20 in Roman numerals, then 40 (XL), 90 (XC), 400 (CD) and 900 (CM).
days.en: Inference: choose a moment when a character makes a big choice. Write what they feel and why, quoting a phrase from the text as evidence.

days.ma: Roman years: decode MCMLXXXV, MMXXIV and MDCLXVI, then write the year you were born and this year in Roman numerals.
days.en: Plan your own myth on a story mountain: a hero, a creature, a quest and a lesson. Note which features you are borrowing from the myth you read.

days.ma: Quick check: count back in 100s from 2,350 to 1,750; what is 100,000 less than 612,004; convert CDXLIV to digits and 1999 to Roman numerals.
days.en: Quick check: retell the myth in 60 words or fewer, turn 'apology', 'solid' and 'active' into verbs, and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Negative numbers and rounding

spell.rule: words ending -cious and -tious (vicious, delicious, ambitious, cautious)

weeks.read: more myths and legends, comparing heroes across stories

days.ma: Draw a number line from −20 to 20 on a long strip of paper. Count back in 3s from 12 to −9 and forward in 5s from −25 to 15.
days.en: Write the opening paragraph of your myth, describing the setting with at least three senses.

days.ma: The freezer is −18 °C and the kitchen is 21 °C: what is the difference? Make up four more temperature pairs that cross zero and find each difference.
days.en: Relative clauses: write five sentences about your myth using who, which, where, when or whose, e.g. 'The cave, which smelt of smoke, was silent.'

days.ma: Round 346,782 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000. Set the answers out in a table and say which rounding changes the most digits.
days.en: Write the middle of your myth where the hero meets the creature. Include a short conversation, punctuated correctly, that shows what each character is like.

days.ma: Find big numbers in a newspaper or reference book (town populations, distances, crowd sizes). Round each to the nearest 1,000 and 10,000 and decide which is most sensible to tell a friend.
days.en: Write the ending, then read the whole myth aloud. Underline two words to improve and check any spelling you are unsure of in a dictionary.

days.ma: Quick check: order −7, 3, −12, 0, −1; find the difference between −6 °C and 9 °C; round 85,549 to the nearest 1,000 and 10,000; give a number that rounds to 400,000.
days.en: Quick check: share your finished myth with the family, point out three relative clauses you used, and spell this week's words from dictation.

weeks.title: Number puzzles and problems

spell.rule: words ending -cial and -tial (official, special, partial, essential)

weeks.read: a news article written for children (printed or online)

days.ma: Puzzle: I am a 6-digit even number; I round to 250,000 to the nearest 10,000 and my digits add to 12. Find two possible numbers, then write a puzzle for a parent.
days.en: Read a news article for children. Mark who, what, where, when and why with five different symbols or colours.

days.ma: Find the population of your town or a nearby city in a reference book or online. Write it in words, round it to the nearest 100,000 and compare it with another place.
days.en: Fact or opinion: sort ten sentences from the article into facts you could check and opinions someone believes. Look for clue words such as 'should', 'best' and 'I think'.

days.ma: A stadium holds 52,305 people. 10,000 seats are added, then 1,000 removed. How many now? Show how the digits change on a place value grid.
days.en: Parenthesis: add extra information with brackets, dashes or commas, e.g. 'The mayor (who arrived late) cut the ribbon.' Write two sentences with each.

days.ma: Negative number problems: a lift at floor 4 goes down 7 floors; it was −3 °C at midnight and rose 11 degrees by noon. Solve these, then write and solve three of your own.
days.en: Plan a news report about a real family or neighbourhood event: headline, a who-what-where-when opening, details, a quote and a closing line.

days.ma: Quick check: round 709,512 to the nearest 100,000; 10,000 less than 203,450; −4 + 9; write 560,070 in words; is 49,999 nearer 40,000 or 50,000?
days.en: Quick check: label five new sentences as fact or opinion, add parenthesis to 'My sister ate the last biscuit', and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Adding and subtracting large numbers

spell.rule: words ending -ant, -ance, -ancy (observant, observance, hesitancy, tolerance)

weeks.read: news reports and the front page of a local paper

days.ma: Column addition: 45,678 + 23,594 and 127,309 + 68,795. Say each carried digit aloud as you go.
days.en: Write a catchy headline and the opening paragraph of your news report, answering who, what, where and when in two sentences.

days.ma: Column subtraction with exchanging: 82,403 − 37,658 and 100,000 − 46,275. Check each answer by adding it to the number you subtracted.
days.en: Write the main body in two paragraphs linked by phrases such as 'Later that afternoon', 'Meanwhile' or 'As a result'.

days.ma: Mental methods: 34,000 + 27,000; 6,450 − 1,999 (take 2,000, add 1); 72,500 + 8,600. Explain your method for each.
days.en: Add a quote from an eyewitness in inverted commas, a subheading, and a caption for an imagined photo.

days.ma: Holiday budget: with £3,000 to spend, add made-up costs (flights £1,248, hotel £975, trips £386) in columns and find how much is left.
days.en: Proof-read using a dictionary: look up any doubtful word by its first three or four letters, and check every verb stays in the past tense.
Quick check: read your report aloud like a newsreader, then point to one example of parenthesis and one linking phrase; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Estimating and multi-step problems

spell.rule: words ending -ent, -ence, -ency (innocent, innocence, frequency, confident)

weeks.read: poems with vivid imagery, e.g. weather or nature poems

days.ma: Round to the nearest 1,000 to estimate 38,912 + 21,207 and 75,003 − 48,699, then calculate. How close was each estimate?
days.en: Read three poems aloud from a poetry anthology. Choose a favourite and give two reasons for your choice.

days.ma: Spot the mistake: a parent writes 24,615 + 18,390 = 52,005 and two correct sums. Use rounding to find the wrong one without working them all out.
days.en: Figurative language hunt: find a simile, a metaphor and an example of personification. Explain what picture each puts in your head.

days.ma: A school raised £2,345 at a fair and £1,870 at a concert, then spent £3,199 on books. How much is left? Draw a bar model first.
days.en: Split two unfamiliar words from the poems into prefix, root and suffix (e.g. un-predict-able) and work out their meaning before checking.

days.ma: Write your own two-step word problem using numbers from home (steps walked in a week, pages read this month). Swap with a parent and solve each other's.
days.en: Start learning a short poem (8–12 lines) by heart: read it aloud three times, then cover one line at a time and recite.

days.ma: Quick check: 8,400 + 5,700 mentally; estimate then calculate 61,248 − 29,875; a library had 14,506 books, gave away 2,380 and bought 1,145 – how many now?
days.en: Quick check: perform your poem using pace, volume and pauses, then name one simile or metaphor and its effect; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Consolidation: number and calculation

spell.rule: review: this half term's prefixes and suffixes (-ate, -ise, -ify, -cious, -tial, -ance, -ence)

weeks.read: finish the half-term novel and write a short recommendation

days.ma: Draw six digit slips to build a number; read it, write it in words and round it to the nearest 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000. Repeat three times.
days.en: Choose your best piece from this half term (myth or news report). Re-read it and use a coloured pen to improve three word choices.

days.ma: Convert MMXV and CCCXC; find the difference between −14 °C and 6 °C; count back in 4s from 10 to −14.
days.en: Find and label in your own writing a relative clause, an expanded noun phrase, parenthesis and a word with a prefix.

days.ma: Column methods: 147,836 + 52,479 and 300,402 − 156,875. Check each with the inverse operation.
days.en: Proof-read a paragraph a parent writes with ten deliberate mistakes (spellings, capital letters, commas, tense). Can you find them all?

days.ma: A charity needs £50,000. It raised £18,765 in spring and £23,490 in summer. How much more does it need? Use rounding to check your answer.
days.en: Book talk: discuss your novel with a parent for 10 minutes. Each of you must build on the other's point ('Yes, and also…') or politely disagree.

days.ma: Half-term check: write 406,060 in words; round 671,500 to the nearest 10,000; −8 + 15; 64,709 + 28,856; 90,000 − 43,618; MCMXC in digits. Mark together and note one thing to revisit.
days.en: Quick check: write a five-sentence recommendation of your book for a friend, with reasons, and take a test on the half term's spelling words.

weeks.title: Multiples and factors

spell.rule: -able and -ible (adorable, possible, reliable, sensible)

weeks.read: an extract from a classic story written over a hundred years ago

days.ma: Arrange 36 pieces of dried pasta into rectangles to find every factor pair: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, 6 × 6.
days.en: Read an extract from a classic story written over a hundred years ago. List words and phrases that sound old-fashioned.

days.ma: List all the factors of 24 and of 40 and circle the common factors. Which is the highest common factor?
days.en: Dictionary detectives: look up five unfamiliar words from the extract using their first three or four letters, and write each meaning in modern English.

days.ma: List the first ten multiples of 6 and of 8. Which numbers appear in both lists? What is the smallest?
days.en: Word roots: find word families (sign, signal, signature; act, action, react) and use known roots to guess new words in the extract.

days.ma: Factor detective: which number under 50 has the most factors? Test 24, 36 and 48 and justify your answer.
days.en: Summarise the extract in three sentences, one per main event, then write two questions you would like answered by reading on.

days.ma: Quick check: all factor pairs of 60; common factors of 18 and 27; a common multiple of 4 and 5; true or false: 7 is a factor of 84.
days.en: Quick check: rewrite two old-fashioned sentences in modern English, find three words in a dictionary against the clock, and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Primes, squares and cubes

spell.rule: -ably and -ibly (considerably, comfortably, horribly, sensibly)

weeks.read: persuasive leaflets, adverts and letters found around the house

days.ma: With pasta pieces, try to make rectangles of 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13 (only one row works – these are prime), then 4, 6, 9 and 12 (composite).
days.en: Collect two leaflets or adverts. Find the persuasive tricks: questions to the reader, exaggeration, 'you' language, and facts mixed with opinions.

days.ma: Write 1–100 in a 10 × 10 grid. Cross out multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 (but not those numbers themselves); circle the primes left and learn those up to 19.
days.en: Modal verbs and adverbs: rewrite 'You will love it' to show different levels of certainty using might, could, should, must, perhaps and definitely.

days.ma: Build squares from coins: 1², 2², 3², 4², 5². Write the squares up to 12² and spot the pattern in the differences (3, 5, 7…).
days.en: Plan a persuasive letter to the family: why we should have a weekly games night. Note three reasons, each backed by evidence.

days.ma: Stack sugar cubes, dice or building bricks into 2 × 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 × 3 cubes. Write 1³ to 5³ (1, 8, 27, 64, 125). What is 10³?
days.en: Write the letter in four paragraphs, using a modal verb in each and answering one objection ('Some might say… however…').

days.ma: Quick check: is 51 prime? (try 3); list the primes up to 19; 7²; 4³; write 30 as a product of prime factors.
days.en: Quick check: read your letter aloud persuasively and let the family vote, then label five sentences fact or opinion; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Mental multiplication and dividing by 10, 100, 1,000

spell.rule: adding suffixes to words ending in -fer (referring, referred, reference, preferred, transferring)

weeks.read: a novel suitable for a family debate about a character's choices

days.ma: If 7 × 8 = 56, what are 70 × 8, 7 × 800, 560 ÷ 8 and 5,600 ÷ 70? Make a fact web for 6 × 9 in the same way.
days.en: Choose a debate question about a book, e.g. 'Was the main character right to break the rules?' Write three reasons for and three against.

days.ma: Draw a place value chart from thousands to thousandths. Show the digits moving for 34 × 10, 34 × 100, 34 × 1,000, 4.5 × 100 and 260 ÷ 1,000.
days.en: Find two quotations from the book that support your side. Practise 'I think… because… for example, on page…'.

days.ma: Mental strategies: 25 × 16 (double and halve), 99 × 6 (100 × 6 − 6), 15 × 12 (15 × 10 + 15 × 2). Explain each method aloud.
days.en: Hold a 10-minute family debate: each person speaks for one minute from notes and replies courteously ('I see your point, but…').

days.ma: A recipe uses 0.25 kg of flour per batch: how much for 10 and 100 batches? A 2 litre bottle is shared into 10 and then 100 equal cups: how much in each?
days.en: Write a short discussion text: introduction, arguments for, arguments against and your conclusion, using 'On the other hand' and 'Furthermore'.
Quick check: give a one-minute talk from notes about your current book, with two reasons and one piece of evidence; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Written multiplication

spell.rule: hyphens after a prefix when two vowels meet (co-ordinate, re-enter, co-operate, co-own)

weeks.read: instructions and explanations: recipes, game rules, how-to guides

days.ma: Short multiplication: 2,347 × 6 and 4,058 × 7 in columns. Estimate first (2,000 × 6) to check the size of the answer.
days.en: Read a recipe or game rules. List the features: title, a 'You will need:' list, numbered steps, bossy (imperative) verbs and time words.

days.ma: Work out 36 × 24 with a grid first, then with formal long multiplication (36 × 4 plus 36 × 20). Compare the two.
days.en: Write a 'You will need:' list for making a sandwich, introducing it with a colon and punctuating the bullet points consistently.

days.ma: Long multiplication: 147 × 32 and 253 × 46. Check with an estimate such as 150 × 30 = 4,500.
days.en: Write instructions for a game or simple recipe you know, with a title, headings, numbered steps and a 'top tip' box.

days.ma: A school orders 28 boxes of 144 pencils; a hall has 36 rows of 24 chairs. Solve both with long multiplication.
days.en: Make a final copy on card: print the title clearly and use joined handwriting for the steps; choose a pen or pencil and explain why.

days.ma: Quick check: 3,219 × 8; 64 × 37; 1,205 × 13; find the error in a worked example where the zero placeholder was forgotten.
days.en: Quick check: a parent follows your instructions exactly – note where they get stuck and add one clearer step; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Short division and remainders

spell.rule: ei after c and the ee sound (receive, ceiling, deceive) plus exceptions (protein, seize)

weeks.read: a story with a strongly described, atmospheric setting

days.ma: Share 96 pasta pieces into 4 equal groups, then write it as short division: 96 ÷ 4 = 24. Repeat with 156 ÷ 6.
days.en: Read a descriptive passage from your book. Collect words and phrases that build atmosphere and sort them by sense.

days.ma: Short division: 4,536 ÷ 7 and 2,913 ÷ 3. Check each by multiplying back.
days.en: Use a thesaurus to find three sharper words each for 'cold', 'dark', 'quiet' and 'walked'; discuss the small differences in meaning.

days.ma: 1,247 ÷ 5 = 249 r 2. Write the remainder as a remainder and as a fraction (249 2/5). Do the same for 863 ÷ 4.
days.en: Look out of a window at dusk; write a paragraph with expanded noun phrases and one piece of personification.

days.ma: Remainders in real life: 130 pupils, 8 per minibus – how many minibuses? (round up). £50 for £6 tickets – how many tickets? (round down).
days.en: Rewrite your paragraph to change the atmosphere from calm to tense, keeping the same setting. Compare which words you changed.

days.ma: Quick check: 3,456 ÷ 8; 925 ÷ 4 with remainder; 2,000 eggs into boxes of 6 – how many full boxes and how many eggs left over?
days.en: Quick check: read both versions aloud; can a parent tell which is calm and which tense, and which words gave it away? Spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Solving problems with all four operations

spell.rule: the letter string ough (ought, bough, rough, cough, though, through, thorough)

weeks.read: a short playscript

days.ma: The equals sign means 'has the same value as': solve 45 + ? = 60 − 7; 6 × 8 = 4 × ?; 120 ÷ ? = 3 × 5. Make up three of your own.
days.en: Read a short playscript. List its features: cast list, scene headings, stage directions in brackets and no speech marks.

days.ma: Six friends share 3 pizzas cut into 8 slices each; then 4 more friends arrive. Can the slices still be shared equally? Use factors to explain.
days.en: Turn a page of dialogue from your book into a playscript, adding stage directions with adverbs (angrily, under her breath).

days.ma: A square patio has an area of 64 m² – how long is each side? A box holds 5³ cubes – how many? Which square number lies between 50 and 60?
days.en: Rehearse your scene with family members, trying different tones and volumes so the meaning is clear.

days.ma: A café sells 148 cups of tea a day at £2 and 96 cakes at £3. What are its takings for a 6-day week? Write the steps before calculating.
days.en: Edit your script after the rehearsal: cut lines that didn't work, add stage directions, and label one verb, adverb and clause.

days.ma: Quick check: buses leave every 12 minutes and trains every 15 from 9:00 – when do both next leave together? 7 × 6 = 50 − ?; 4² + 2³; change from £20 after 3 books at £4.75.
days.en: Quick check: perform the scene for the family, then explain one change you made to the script and why; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Consolidation: multiplication and division

spell.rule: review: -able/-ible, -fer words, hyphenated prefixes, ei and ough

weeks.read: a winter poem or seasonal story, read aloud

days.ma: Sort 2, 9, 15, 17, 21, 25, 29, 36, 49 and 51 into primes, square numbers and other composite numbers. Explain 51.
days.en: Pick your best writing from this half term (letter, instructions or description) and improve three words using a thesaurus.

days.ma: Long multiplication: 342 × 24 and 1,506 × 7. Estimate first, then calculate.
days.en: Homophones: write sentences for there/their/they're, where/wear/were and its/it's, then proof-read your chosen piece for them.

days.ma: Short division: 2,748 ÷ 6 and 5,003 ÷ 4. If 5,003 guests sit at tables of 4, how many tables are needed?
days.en: Make a neat final copy of your improved piece in joined handwriting.

days.ma: Powers of 10 relay: a parent calls out 6.3 × 100, 4,200 ÷ 1,000, 0.57 × 10, 80 ÷ 100; you answer and show it on a place value chart.
days.en: Learn a short winter poem by heart (or polish your autumn poem) and rehearse it with expression.

days.ma: Half-term check: factor pairs of 48; is 91 prime?; 6³; 2,435 × 6; 57 × 34; 3,148 ÷ 4; 0.72 × 100; 8 = 64 ÷ ?. Mark together and note one thing to revisit.
days.en: Quick check: perform your poem to the family and take a test on the half term's spelling words.

weeks.title: Equivalent fractions and ordering

spell.rule: silent letters (doubt, island, lamb, solemn, knight, psalm)

weeks.read: a biography of an inspiring person from history (non-fiction)

days.ma: Fold paper strips into halves, quarters and eighths; show that 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. Write every fraction equal to 1/2 up to twelfths.
days.en: Read a short biography from the library or a children's encyclopedia. Make a timeline of five key events in the person's life.

days.ma: Shade 3/10 on a 10 × 10 grid and show it equals 30/100. Find hundredths equal to 7/10, 1/5 and 1/4.
days.en: Make a fact file with notes (not sentences) under headings: early life, achievements, challenges, why they are remembered.

days.ma: Simplify 6/8, 9/12, 15/20 and 40/100 by dividing top and bottom by a common factor.
days.en: Perfect form: change 'She won the prize' to 'She had won the prize before she was twenty' and 'She has inspired many people'. Write four sentences of your own.

days.ma: Order 2/3, 5/6 and 7/12 (change to twelfths), then 3/4, 5/8 and 11/16. Draw bars to check.
days.en: Silent letter hunt: find words with silent letters in your book or around the house (knee, comb, scissors, wrist) and group them by silent letter.

days.ma: Quick check: three fractions equal to 2/5; simplify 18/24; order 1/2, 3/8, 5/16; which is greater, 7/10 or 69/100?
days.en: Quick check: tell a parent five facts about the person from memory, write two sentences in the perfect form, and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Mixed numbers and improper fractions

spell.rule: more silent letters (gnome, rhubarb, column, autumn, sword)

weeks.read: an autobiography or memoir extract, plus a family member's life story

days.ma: Cut paper circles into quarters. Show 7/4 as seven quarters, then rearrange it as 1 3/4. Do the same with 9/4 and 11/4.
days.en: Interview a grandparent, neighbour or family member about their life, noting answers to six questions you prepare.

days.ma: Convert 13/5, 17/3 and 25/8 to mixed numbers, and 2 3/4, 3 1/6 and 4 2/5 to improper fractions.
days.en: Plan a biography of them with paragraphs for early life, key events and life now; give each paragraph a heading.

days.ma: Draw a number line from 0 to 4 marked in thirds. Place 5/3, 2 1/3, 10/3 and 3 2/3 on it.
days.en: Write the biography in the third person and past tense, linking paragraphs with 'Years later', 'After that' and 'Eventually'.

days.ma: Write statements such as 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 = 1 2/5. Make five of your own where the total is more than 1.
days.en: Edit for consistent tense and subject–verb agreement ('they were', not 'they was'); add a fact box. Use root words to explain 'autobiography' (auto + bio + graph).

days.ma: Quick check: 19/6 as a mixed number; 5 1/2 as an improper fraction; order 9/4, 2 1/8 and 17/8; 4/7 + 5/7.
days.en: Quick check: read the biography to the person you interviewed and ask what you got right; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Adding and subtracting fractions

spell.rule: homophones: advice/advise, device/devise, practice/practise, licence/license (noun -ce, verb -se)

weeks.read: a traditional tale or modern story from another culture

days.ma: Same denominators: 3/8 + 4/8, 7/9 − 2/9, 5/6 + 4/6 (write the last as a mixed number). Show each with paper strips.
days.en: Read a traditional tale from a culture different from your own. Note the setting, foods, customs or words that show where it comes from.

days.ma: Related denominators: 1/2 + 1/4, 2/3 + 1/6 and 3/4 − 3/8. Change to the same denominator first and draw bars.
days.en: Compare it with a fairy tale you know well using a Venn diagram of similarities and differences.

days.ma: Mixed numbers: 2 1/4 + 1 1/2 and 3 5/6 − 1 1/3. Deal with the wholes first, then the fractions.
days.en: Discuss with a parent what the story shows people value (honesty, cleverness, family). Each person must build on the last idea.

days.ma: A cake uses 3/4 cup of sugar and 1/8 cup of honey. How much sweetener in total? If you had 2 cups of sugar, how much is left?
days.en: Homophones: write pairs of sentences with advice/advise and practice/practise, and a memory trick (the noun has 'ice' like 'device').

days.ma: Quick check: 5/12 + 1/3; 1 − 3/10; 4 2/5 − 2 7/10; a 3 1/2 m ribbon has 1 3/4 m cut off – how much is left?
days.en: Quick check: summarise the tale in three sentences, name one theme, complete five homophone gap sentences, and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Multiplying fractions and scaling

spell.rule: near-homophones and often-confused words (affect/effect, aloud/allowed, past/passed, herd/heard)

weeks.read: a story that jumps in time with a flashback

days.ma: Use paper strips to show 3 × 2/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5. Then draw 4 × 3/4 and 5 × 2/3.
days.en: Read a chapter and find where the author refers back to the past. How is it signalled ('had' + verb, 'years before')?

days.ma: Mixed number × whole number: 3 × 1 1/2 and 4 × 2 1/3. Multiply the whole part and fraction part separately, then add.
days.en: Plan a short story with a flashback: a present-day opening, a memory, and a return to the present. Note how the character feels in each part.

days.ma: Scaling: a recipe for 4 needs 1 1/2 cups of flour – how much for 8 and for 12? A model is 1/10 the size of a 4 m car – how long is it?
days.en: Write the present-day opening and the flashback, using the past perfect: 'She had never seen the sea before that summer.'

days.ma: Rates: a tap fills 6 litres a minute – how much in 7 minutes? A cyclist rides 3 km every 10 minutes – how far in an hour? Show it in a table.
days.en: Write the return to the present and an ending that links to the memory. Check affect/effect and past/passed.

days.ma: Quick check: 6 × 3/8; 2 × 2 3/5; 1/4 of 36; a robot moves 5 m every 2 seconds – how far in 20 seconds?
days.en: Quick check: read your story aloud and show where the time changes and which verb forms tell the reader; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Decimals as fractions and thousandths

spell.rule: more often-confused words (stationary/stationery, principal/principle, profit/prophet, wary/weary)

weeks.read: an information book about an animal or place

days.en: Read an information book. Note how it's organised: headings, subheadings, bullet points, diagrams and a glossary.

days.ma: Kitchen scales read 1.235 kg – what does each digit mean? Show that 1 g = 1/1,000 kg = 0.001 kg.
days.en: Précis: summarise one long paragraph in 25 words or fewer, keeping only the key facts.

days.ma: On a place value chart write 0.4, 0.04 and 0.004 and say each as a fraction. How many thousandths make one tenth? One hundredth?
days.en: Plan a report on something you know well (a hobby, a pet, your town) with four subheadings and notes under each.

days.ma: Measure five objects in millimetres (pen, spoon, phone charger…). Write each in metres to three decimal places (154 mm = 0.154 m) and as a fraction.
days.en: Write two sections using a colon to introduce a list and consistent bullet points. Break technical words into parts (sub-marine, tele-scope) to explain them.

days.ma: Quick check: 0.307 as a fraction; 9/1,000 as a decimal; 3 tenths + 4 thousandths; which is bigger, 0.06 or 0.006?
days.en: Quick check: share your report and point out a colon, a bullet list and your précis; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Consolidation: fractions

spell.rule: review: silent letters and homophones

weeks.read: a non-fiction book on a topic of the child's choice, for a short presentation

days.ma: Make a fraction wall from paper strips (halves to twelfths). Use it to find three pairs of equivalent fractions and order 5/6, 3/4 and 2/3.
days.en: Pick your best writing of this half term (biography, flashback story or report). Highlight one strength and one place to improve, then edit it.

days.ma: Convert 23/4 to a mixed number; add 2/3 + 5/6; subtract 1 1/2 − 3/4.
days.en: List five words you misspelt this half term, find the tricky part of each and make up a memory trick.

days.ma: Multiply 7 × 3/5 and 3 × 2 1/4; draw one of them as a bar model.
days.en: Prepare a two-minute talk about your report topic using notes on a small card.

days.ma: Make matching cards: 0.5 and 1/2, 0.25 and 25/100, 0.007 and 7/1,000, 0.43 and 43/100, 0.9 and 9/10. Play pairs face down.
days.en: Give your talk to the family, then answer two questions using your notes.

days.ma: Half-term check: simplify 12/18; order 3/5, 7/10, 13/20; 22/7 as a mixed number; 3/8 + 3/4; 2 − 5/6; 4 × 2/3; 0.063 as a fraction. Mark together and note one thing to revisit.
days.en: Quick check: give an example of a perfect-form verb, a relative clause, a modal verb and parenthesis, then take the half-term spelling test.

weeks.title: Ordering and rounding decimals

spell.rule: double letters in tricky words (accommodate, embarrass, committee, occurrence)

weeks.read: a narrative poem or ballad that tells a story

days.ma: Order 2.45, 2.405, 2.5 and 2.054 using a place value chart, then write comparisons with < and >.
days.en: Read a narrative poem or ballad aloud. Retell its story in your own words.

days.ma: Order packet weights from lightest to heaviest: 0.454 kg, 1.5 kg, 0.75 kg, 1.25 kg, 0.4 kg (or use real packets from the cupboard).
days.en: Tap the beat of one verse and mark the stressed syllables. Discuss how rhythm and rhyme carry the story along.

days.ma: Round 3.46, 7.82, 12.05 and 0.97 to the nearest whole number and to one decimal place. Draw a number line for the trickiest.
days.en: Learn two verses by heart and mark where to speed up, slow down, get louder or quieter.

days.ma: Race times: 12.47 s, 12.5 s, 12.09 s, 12.405 s. Who won? Round each to one decimal place – does any order change?
days.en: Write a fair copy of your favourite verse in your best handwriting and illustrate it; explain your choice of pen or pencil.

days.ma: Quick check: order 0.6, 0.06, 0.66, 0.606; round 4.95 to one decimal place and to a whole number; give a number with three decimal places between 2.3 and 2.31.
days.en: Quick check: perform your verses and name one figurative phrase and its effect; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Calculating with decimals

spell.rule: unstressed vowels you can't hear clearly (separate, desperate, definite, category)

weeks.read: formal letters, notices and official information leaflets

days.ma: Add £3.45 + £12.80 + £0.99 and take £7.65 from £20 in columns, lining up the decimal points.
days.en: Compare an informal note ('Hiya, can't come!') with a formal letter. List differences in words, contractions and greetings.

days.ma: A shelf is 1.2 m long. Three books are 0.035 m, 0.042 m and 0.028 m thick. What is their total thickness and how much shelf is left?
days.en: Formal language: change 'We need to fix the park' to 'It is essential that the park be repaired'. Write four formal requests about your area.

days.ma: Show digits moving on a place value chart for 0.45 × 100, 3.2 ÷ 10, 56 ÷ 1,000 and 0.006 × 1,000.
days.en: Plan a formal letter to the local council about improving something nearby (a crossing, bins, a play area): reason, evidence, suggestion.

days.ma: 100 identical paper clips weigh 0.15 kg – how much does one weigh in kg and in g? Ten apples weigh 1.85 kg – about how much is one?
days.en: Write the letter, then edit for formality: remove slang and contractions, check paragraphs and end with 'Yours faithfully'.

days.ma: Quick check: 4.75 + 2.6; 10 − 3.48; 7.3 × 100; 82 ÷ 1,000; items cost £4.99 and £3.75 – how much change from £10?
days.en: Quick check: turn five informal sentences into formal ones and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Percentages

spell.rule: the 'shun' sound spelt -tion, -sion, -ssion, -cian (explanation, extension, admission, magician)

weeks.read: a science explanation of how something works, e.g. the water cycle

days.ma: On a 10 × 10 grid shade 37 squares: that's 37%, 37/100 and 0.37. Do the same for 5%, 50% and 85%.
days.en: Read an explanation of a natural process such as the water cycle. Draw a labelled flow diagram of the steps.

days.ma: Learn 1/2 = 50% = 0.5, 1/4 = 25%, 1/5 = 20%, 2/5 = 40%, 4/5 = 80%. Make matching cards and play pairs.
days.en: Passive voice: change 'The sun heats the water' to 'The water is heated by the sun'. Write four passive sentences and discuss why scientists use them.

days.ma: Find 50% of £36, 25% of 80, 10% of 450 and 20% of 60 g. Explain the shortcut for each.
days.en: Split evaporation, condensation and precipitation into root and suffix and use the parts to explain each meaning.

days.ma: Find percentages on food packets (e.g. '30% fruit'). What percentage is not fruit? Write it as a fraction and a decimal.
days.en: Write your own explanation of how something at home works (a kettle, a fridge, a bicycle) using because, so, as a result and therefore.

days.ma: Quick check: 3/25 as a percentage; 0.7 as a percentage; 40% of 25; in a class of 20, 15 have a pet – what percentage is that?
days.en: Quick check: explain your process aloud from your diagram, point to two passive sentences, and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Converting units of measure

spell.rule: words from French with unusual endings (-que, -gue, -eur: unique, tongue, amateur)

weeks.read: a mystery or detective story

days.ma: Measure the kitchen table in cm and convert to m and mm; convert 2.5 km to m and 3,400 m to km.
days.en: Read the opening of a mystery. Predict the culprit and copy two clues from the text that support your prediction.

days.ma: Weigh items on kitchen scales and convert grams to kilograms (450 g = 0.45 kg). How many 250 ml cups make 1 litre? 1.5 litres?
days.en: Inference: what does a suspicious character's behaviour suggest? Write 'I think… because the text says…'.

days.ma: Rough equivalents: 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm, 1 foot ≈ 30 cm, 1 pound ≈ 450 g, 1 pint ≈ 570 ml. Measure your height in cm and estimate it in feet and inches.
days.en: Commas for clarity: compare 'Let's eat, Grandma' with 'Let's eat Grandma' and write three sentences where a comma changes the meaning; add hyphens to 'man eating shark'.

days.ma: Convert an old recipe: 1 lb flour, 2 pints milk, 8 oz sugar (1 oz ≈ 28 g) into approximate metric amounts.
days.en: Use a thesaurus to find suspenseful synonyms for 'look' (peer, glance, scrutinise) and 'said' (hissed, whispered); use five in sentences.

days.ma: Quick check: 3.4 km in m; 650 mm in cm; 2,750 g in kg; 1.2 l in ml; roughly how many cm in 12 inches?
days.en: Quick check: update your prediction with new evidence, punctuate three ambiguous sentences, and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Measurement problems, money and rates

spell.rule: the suffixes -ment and -ness, keeping the root (equipment, government, happiness, loneliness)

weeks.read: more mystery stories, looking at how clues are planted

days.ma: Potatoes cost £1.10 per kg and carrots £0.80 per kg. What do 1.2 kg of potatoes and 0.5 kg of carrots cost altogether?
days.en: Plan a short mystery set at home: a missing object, three suspects, a red herring and a final clue.

days.ma: A recipe for 4 uses 300 g pasta, 0.6 l sauce and 150 g cheese. Scale it for 8 people and for 2.
days.en: Write the opening, building suspense with short sentences, a dash for a dramatic pause and a relative clause about a suspect.

days.ma: A car uses 1 litre of fuel every 15 km – how much for 135 km? Walking at 5 km an hour, how long does 12.5 km take?
days.en: Write the middle where clues are found, with dialogue that moves the action on.

days.ma: How many 25 cm tiles fit along a 2 m wall? How much ribbon goes twice round a parcel 30 cm by 20 cm? Give answers in cm and m.
days.en: Write the reveal, then proof-read with a dictionary and check that your commas prevent any confusion.

days.ma: Quick check: 4 × 1.75 kg; £5 ÷ 4; 3 bottles of 750 ml in litres; a plant 4 cm tall grows 1.5 cm a week – how tall after 6 weeks?
days.en: Quick check: read your mystery to the family – can they solve it before the end? Note one edit to make and spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Consolidation: decimals, percentages and measures

spell.rule: review: double letters, unstressed vowels, -tion/-sion and -ment/-ness

weeks.read: a finished book to discuss in a family book club

days.ma: Order 6.035, 6.3, 6.305 and 6.53, then round each to one decimal place and to the nearest whole number.
days.en: Choose your best piece from this half term (formal letter, explanation or mystery) and improve it using a checklist of that text type's features.

days.ma: Complete fraction–decimal–percentage triangles for 1/4, 2/5, 3/10, 0.15 and 64%.
days.en: Book club: discuss a book you've finished with a family member; agree, or courteously challenge each other's views on the ending.

days.ma: Conversion race: 4.2 kg to g; 75 cm to m; 3,500 ml to l; 0.6 km to m. Time yourself, then try to beat it.
days.en: Find and label in your writing a passive sentence, a modal verb, a relative clause and an example of parenthesis.

days.ma: A jug holds 1.5 l. 40% is poured out. How many millilitres remain? Show two ways.
days.en: Proof-read your chosen piece backwards, sentence by sentence, to catch spelling slips.

days.ma: Half-term check: 0.47 as a percentage; 3/5 as a decimal; order 0.9, 0.09, 0.909; round 13.86 to one decimal place; 2.4 m in cm; 25% of 1.2 kg in g; £10 − £6.37. Mark and note one thing to revisit.
days.en: Quick check: a two-minute book talk from notes, then the half-term spelling test.

weeks.title: Perimeter and area

spell.rule: words ending -sure and -ture (measure, treasure, creature, adventure)

weeks.read: opinion columns and discussion texts on one topic

days.ma: Measure a rectangular table and a book in cm; calculate the perimeter and area (cm²) of each.
days.en: Read two opinion pieces on the same topic (e.g. homework, screen time). List facts and opinions in two columns.

days.ma: On squared paper draw an L-shaped room: 8 m by 6 m with a 3 m by 2 m corner cut out. Find the missing lengths and the perimeter.
days.en: Write two sentences joined by a semi-colon ('It was raining; we stayed in') and two using a colon to explain ('There was one problem: the door was locked').

days.ma: Find the area of the L-shape by splitting it into two rectangles – then do it a different way to check.
days.en: Plan a balanced argument: 'Should 10-year-olds have their own mobile phone?' Three points for each side with evidence.

days.ma: Draw round your hand on 1 cm squared paper. Estimate the area by counting whole squares and squares more than half covered.
days.en: Write it with an introduction, both sides and a reasoned conclusion, using 'However', 'In addition' and 'On balance'.

days.ma: Quick check: perimeter and area of a 7 cm × 4 cm rectangle; a square with perimeter 36 cm – what is its area?; two different rectangles with area 24 cm².
days.en: Quick check: hold a five-minute family debate on the topic, each side giving reasons; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Volume, capacity and time

spell.rule: y making an 'i' sound in words from Greek (myth, gym, pyramid, mystery)

weeks.read: a finished book plus a few book reviews

days.ma: Build cuboids from sugar cubes, dice or building bricks; count the cubes and record length × width × height each time.
days.en: Read two book reviews (newspaper, magazine or library leaflet). List their features: summary without spoilers, opinion, rating and recommendation.

days.ma: Estimate, then measure, how many cups fill a jug; read the scale in ml. Estimate the capacity of a mug, a bowl and a bottle and check.
days.en: Plan a review of a book you've finished: who would enjoy it and why, the best moment, and one criticism.

days.ma: Convert: 2.5 hours to minutes, 4 minutes to seconds, 3 days to hours, 6 weeks to days. How many days in a leap year?
days.en: Make review words with suffixes -ful, -less, -able and -ous (suspenseful, believable, humorous); check spellings with a dictionary.

days.ma: A film starts at 17:45 and lasts 2 h 15 min – when does it end? About how many days old are you? Show your working.
days.en: Write the review in four paragraphs with a star rating and a reason for it.

days.ma: Quick check: volume of a 3 × 2 × 4 cuboid of cubes; 400 ml + 750 ml in litres; 3 h 20 min in minutes; 200 seconds in minutes and seconds; 72 hours in days.
days.en: Quick check: recommend the book to a family member in one minute, justifying your rating; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Measuring and drawing angles

spell.rule: prefixes sub-, inter-, super-, anti-, auto- and what they mean

weeks.read: a story told as a diary or in the first person

days.ma: Find angles around the house: corner of a book (right angle), open scissors (acute), a wide-open door (obtuse), the outside of a corner (reflex). Sort them.
days.en: Read diary entries in a story. How do the first person and informal language show the writer's feelings?

days.ma: Fold a scrap of paper twice to make a right-angle checker; test ten angles in the room and estimate each in degrees.
days.en: Choose a character from your book at a dramatic moment. Infer their thoughts and feelings and list evidence from the text.

days.ma: Draw angles of 40°, 75°, 130° and 160° using a protractor (from a school pencil case if you have one). Label each acute or obtuse.
days.en: Write a diary entry as that character in the first person, using modal verbs to show worries ('I might never…').

days.ma: A parent draws five angles; estimate each, then measure it. Score a point for every estimate within 10°.
days.en: Edit: keep the tense and first person consistent; change one sentence to show emotion through actions rather than naming it.

days.ma: Quick check: name the type of 95°, 270° and 17°; draw 60°; what angle do clock hands make at 2 o'clock and at 4 o'clock?
days.en: Quick check: read your diary aloud in character while a parent asks two questions in role; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Angles on a line, at a point and in rectangles

spell.rule: words ending -ous (dangerous, various, courageous, outrageous)

weeks.read: a collection of poems on one theme, e.g. the sea or the city

days.ma: Cross two pencils on paper and draw along them. Measure or reason the four angles; show angles on a straight line total 180° and round a point 360°.
days.en: Read three poems on one theme. Pick the line with the strongest image and explain its effect on you.

days.ma: Missing angles: a straight line split into 65° and ?; angles round a point of 90°, 120° and ?. How many degrees in a quarter, half and three-quarter turn?
days.en: Gather ideas for your own poem on that theme: list sights, sounds and smells, and turn three into similes or metaphors.

days.ma: Measure a rectangular card: opposite sides equal, all angles 90°. If a rectangle's long side is 12 cm and perimeter 34 cm, find the short side.
days.en: Draft a poem of three or four verses, using a thesaurus to find precise verbs.

days.ma: Draw a rectangle and one diagonal. If the diagonal makes a 35° angle at one corner, find the other part of that corner. Make up three more.
days.en: Read the poem aloud to test its rhythm, cut unnecessary words and write a neat final copy.

days.ma: Quick check: missing angle on a line with 112°; round a point with 150° and 95°; a rectangle 9 cm long with perimeter 30 cm – how wide?; right angles in a full turn?
days.en: Quick check: perform your poem using pauses and emphasis; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Polygons and 3-D shapes

spell.rule: word families that reveal silent letters (sign/signature, muscle/muscular, bomb/bombard)

weeks.read: reference books and children's information websites for a research project

days.ma: Draw a square, a rectangle, a regular hexagon and an irregular pentagon with a ruler. Measure sides and angles to explain which are regular.
days.en: Choose a research question (e.g. 'How do bees make honey?') and find two sources: a library book, an encyclopedia or a children's website.

days.ma: Hunt for 3-D shapes at home: cereal box (cuboid), tin (cylinder), dice (cube). Sketch each and count faces, edges and vertices.
days.en: Take notes in your own words under headings, recording where each fact came from.

days.ma: Open a small box flat and draw its net. Then draw two different nets of a cube on squared paper, cut them out and fold to test.
days.en: Turn your notes into a poster with headings, bullet points and a colon before a list; print the headings clearly.

days.ma: Make a triangular dotty grid on paper and draw a cube and a cuboid on it. Ask a parent to name 3-D shapes from your drawings.
days.en: Rehearse a three-minute presentation from your poster, keeping to the topic and using notes.

days.ma: Quick check: is a rhombus regular? Why?; name the shape with six rectangular faces; vertices on a square-based pyramid; sketch a net of a cuboid.
days.en: Quick check: give your presentation and answer questions; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Consolidation: measurement and geometry

spell.rule: review: -sure/-ture, y as 'i', -ous and science prefixes

weeks.read: two favourite books from the year so far, to compare

days.ma: Draw a shape made of two rectangles; find its perimeter and area.
days.en: Choose your best writing this half term (argument, review, diary or poem) and judge it against its purpose: does it do its job?

days.ma: Write your name in capital letters with a ruler; estimate then measure the angles in letters such as A, K, N and V.
days.en: Proof-read your chosen piece with a dictionary, finding any doubtful word by its first three or four letters.

days.ma: Estimate how many cubes would build a 2 × 3 × 4 cuboid, then calculate. Pour exactly 350 ml into a jug and read the scale.
days.en: Grammar quiz with a parent: give an example of a semi-colon, a colon, a modal verb, a relative clause, the passive and the perfect form.

days.ma: Sort household shapes into regular and irregular polygons. Find the missing angle round a point: 100°, 80°, 110° and ?.
days.en: Compare two books you've read this year: which had the better ending and why? Listen and respond to a parent's view.

days.ma: Half-term check: perimeter and area of 6 cm × 9 cm; volume of a 4 × 4 × 4 cube; 90 minutes in hours; type of a 200° angle; missing angle on a line with 47°; is every rectangle regular? Mark and note one thing to revisit.
days.en: Quick check: the half-term spelling test, then write a final copy of your improved piece.

weeks.title: Reflection and translation

spell.rule: adverbs from adjectives ending -ic and -le (basically, frantically, gently, terribly)

weeks.read: an adventure or quest story

days.ma: Fold paper, cut a shape and open it to see the reflection. On squared paper, reflect a triangle in a vertical mirror line.
days.en: Read an adventure story chapter; note how the author builds tension and reveals the hero's character.

days.ma: Draw axes numbered 0–10 and plot a triangle at (2, 3), (5, 3), (2, 7). Reflect it in the line x = 6 and write the new coordinates.
days.en: Plan your own adventure: a map of the setting, a hero with a strength and a flaw, three obstacles and a climax.

days.ma: Slide a paper shape on squared paper 4 squares right and 3 down; describe the move in words and record the new coordinates.
days.en: Write character profiles of your hero and villain using expanded noun phrases and relative clauses.

days.ma: Design a border pattern by translating and reflecting one simple shape. Explain why the shape's size and angles never change.
days.en: Build word families from roots (venture → adventure, adventurous; brave → bravery, bravely) and check spellings.

days.ma: Quick check: reflect a rectangle in a mirror line; translate (1, 2) 3 right and 4 up; describe the move from (5, 5) to (2, 8).
days.en: Quick check: tell your story plan aloud in two minutes; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Line graphs

spell.rule: words ending -er, -or, -ar (sailor, calendar, collar, governor)

weeks.read: adventure stories, noticing how chapters end on a cliffhanger

days.ma: A parent sketches a line graph of temperature from 6 am to 6 pm. Find the highest and lowest and the rise between two times.
days.en: Write the opening of your adventure, introducing setting and hero with a strong hook.

days.ma: Collect data: measure the length of a shadow from a pencil standing on a sunny windowsill every hour (or a seedling's height every day).
days.en: Write the build-up and problem, with dialogue that reveals character.

days.ma: Draw a line graph of your data with labelled axes and a sensible scale.
days.en: Write the climax using a mix of short and long sentences and a dash for drama.

days.ma: Write and answer five questions about your graph: how much did it change between two times? When was the change fastest? What is the total of two readings?
days.en: Write the resolution, then edit for tense, subject–verb agreement and silent-letter spellings.

days.ma: Quick check: from a parent's line graph of a car journey (distance against time), answer three comparison and difference questions.
days.en: Quick check: read your adventure aloud to the family; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Tables and timetables

spell.rule: plurals of words ending -f, -fe and -o (halves, knives, potatoes, pianos)

weeks.read: a magazine or newspaper feature article

days.ma: Read a bus or train timetable (printed or online). Find how long three journeys take and which bus gets you somewhere by 10:00.
days.en: Read a magazine feature. Note how headings, a standfirst, captions and fact boxes guide the reader.

days.ma: Make a 24-hour timetable for a family day out: leave 08:45, travel 1 h 20 min, activities and lunch, home by 17:30.
days.en: Retrieve: make a table of five key facts from the feature with the paragraph each came from.

days.ma: Make a table of family members' heights in cm (or shoe sizes). Ask and answer: who is tallest? What is the difference between the tallest and shortest?
days.en: Write a feature article about your adventure story's setting as if it were a real place, with headings and a fact box.

days.ma: Your 14:35 train is 25 minutes late and the journey takes 1 h 50 min – when do you arrive? Convert 7:20 pm and 11:05 am to the 24-hour clock.
days.en: Add brackets or dashes for extra information and bullet points with a colon; check one fact and one opinion are clearly marked.

days.ma: Quick check: from the timetable, the journey time between two stops; 19:40 in 12-hour time; 135 minutes in hours and minutes; a fact read from your height table.
days.en: Quick check: share your article and point out one fact, one opinion and one piece of parenthesis; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Problem-solving with the whole year's maths

spell.rule: suffixes -ful, -less, -ly keeping the root (hopeful, careless, carefully)

weeks.read: speeches and persuasive talks

days.ma: Party planning: 28 guests, sandwiches in packs of 6 at £1.85 – how many packs and what cost? Show each step.
days.en: Read or listen to a speech for children. Note how the speaker uses questions, repetition and pauses.

days.ma: Ages puzzle: Mum is 3 times Sam's age; in 6 years their ages will add up to 60. How old is each now? Try and improve guesses in a table.
days.en: Choose a topic you care about (e.g. less litter in the park) and write a two-minute speech with three reasons.

days.ma: Square and cube clues: I'm a square number and a multiple of 4 between 30 and 70. I'm a cube number less than 100 that is odd. Who am I?
days.en: Word study: use roots to explain 'visible, invisible, vision' and 'export, transport, portable'; add one to your speech.

days.ma: A family drives 238 km at an average of 68 km per hour, stopping for 25 minutes. Leaving at 09:10, when do they arrive?
days.en: Rehearse your speech with notes, using gestures, volume and eye contact.

days.ma: Quick check: 3,000 − (465 + 1,280); 15 × 24; 2,345 ÷ 5; how many 0.25 l glasses from 3 litres; round 487,654 to the nearest 10,000.
days.en: Quick check: deliver your speech to the family, who must ask one question you answer with a reason; spell this week's words.

weeks.title: Review: number, calculation and fractions

spell.rule: review: tricky statutory words from the year

weeks.read: a short story read in one sitting, then a non-fiction extract on the same theme

days.ma: Read and write 703,060 and 730,600 in words; round both to the nearest 1,000 and 100,000; add them with the column method.
days.en: Read a short story in one sitting. Write three questions about it: one 'find it' question, one 'why' question, one 'what does this word mean' question, and answer them.

days.ma: Long multiplication 256 × 37 and short division 6,174 ÷ 6; check each with an estimate.
days.en: Find two examples of figurative language in the story and explain the effect on the reader.

days.ma: Fractions: 2/3 + 5/12; 3 1/4 − 1 5/8; 5 × 3/4 as a mixed number.
days.en: Read a non-fiction extract on the same theme and sort five statements from it into facts and opinions.

days.ma: Percentages: 20% of £45, 75% of 120, 40% of 2.5 kg; write 3/20 and 7/25 as percentages.
days.en: Retrieve and present: turn the extract's key facts into a five-bullet fact box with a heading.

days.ma: Quick check: ten mixed questions – place value, rounding, column methods, long multiplication, division with remainder, fractions and percentages. Mark and talk about the trickiest.
days.en: Quick check: summarise the story in 40 words, explain one unfamiliar word using its root, and take a spelling test of words from the year.

weeks.title: Review: measurement, geometry and statistics

spell.rule: review: the year's spelling rules (prefixes, suffixes, homophones, silent letters)

weeks.read: a mix of poems and short non-fiction pieces to spot grammar features in

days.ma: Measure and convert: the length of the hallway in m and cm; a bag of shopping in kg and g; a glass of water in ml and l.
days.en: Grammar treasure hunt: find in a book a relative clause, a modal verb, a passive sentence, parenthesis and a perfect-form verb.

days.ma: Area of the floor of your bedroom in m² (measure and multiply); estimate how many 50 cm × 50 cm squares would cover it.
days.en: Punctuation fix-up: a parent writes five sentences missing commas, brackets, dashes, a colon or a semi-colon; you correct them.

days.ma: Draw and measure angles of 25°, 90°, 145° and 210°; find missing angles on a line (138°) and round a point (90°, 115°, ?).
days.en: Prefix and suffix challenge: make as many words as you can from the root 'act' or 'form' in five minutes.

days.ma: Plot a square at (1, 1), (3, 1), (3, 3), (1, 3); translate it 4 right and 2 up and reflect it in a vertical line; record coordinates.
days.en: Homophone and confused-word quiz: advice/advise, affect/effect, stationary/stationery, principal/principle.

days.ma: Quick check: read a parent's line graph of daily temperatures and answer two difference questions; convert 3.6 kg to g and 450 cm to m; area of a 12 m × 7 m garden.
days.en: Quick check: use grammar terms to explain three sentences you wrote this year, and spell ten of the year's words.

weeks.title: Fun project: plan a family fun day

spell.rule: spell-it-right: words for your fun day programme

weeks.read: the child's free choice, including a book to recommend for the summer holiday

days.ma: Plan a family fun day with a pretend budget of £50: list activities and food with prices and make sure the total stays within budget.
days.en: Plan a fun day programme: the audience (the family), the purpose (inform and excite), and the sections you will include.

days.ma: Make a timetable for the day in 24-hour time, with start and end times and how long each event lasts.
days.en: Write the programme: a welcome paragraph, a timetable, a description of each activity and the rules for a quiz or game.

days.ma: Work out scores and prizes: if 20% of points are bonus points, how many bonus points are in a 40-point game? Round the money spent to check it.
days.en: Edit and proof-read the programme, then make a neat final copy with headings and bullet points; choose the best pen for each part.

days.ma: Hold the fun day (or part of it): measure and record results in a table – longest standing jump in cm, beanbag throws, a timed puzzle.
days.en: Write and rehearse a short opening speech or a poem to perform at the start of the fun day.

days.ma: Final check: present the results table and answer questions about it – who won each event and by how much?
days.en: Perform your speech or poem, then recommend one book for the summer holiday and explain why.
